# x0k-release-metadata

A program that updates itself downloads its next release from servers it
does not control. Before it installs that release, it has to decide from the
bytes alone that the people who maintain it signed this release, for this
machine, and that nobody handed it an old or a withheld one instead.

`x0k-release-metadata` makes that decision. It is one Rust crate with one pure
function, `verify`, and the commands maintainers use to sign. The metadata is
[TUF](https://theupdateframework.io)'s, with two additions:

- **A threshold counts people, not keys.** A maintainer who holds a laptop
  key, a security key and a phone passkey is one signatory. A root that needs
  two signatories needs two people.
- **Hardware keys sign directly.** A signature may be an SSHSIG envelope, the
  format `ssh-keygen -Y sign` writes. So a FIDO2 security key, a Secure Enclave
  key through [Secretive](https://github.com/maxgoedjen/secretive), a phone's
  passkey and an ordinary SSH key can all sign a release. A signatory's rule
  can demand that a person touched the token.

A repository that uses neither addition is plain TUF, and stock TUF clients
read it the same way.

## Verify a release

```toml
[dependencies]
x0k-release-metadata = "0.3"
```

```rust
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::time::SystemTime;
use x0k_release_metadata::{verify, Artifact, Fetched, TrustedState};

// What this machine trusted after its last update: at first, the root it shipped with.
let trusted = TrustedState::from_root(std::fs::read("trusted/root.json")?);
// What you fetched, your own way: newer roots in order, the timestamp, the
// snapshot, and each targets file by role name.
let fetched = Fetched {
    roots: vec![],
    timestamp: std::fs::read("timestamp.json")?,
    snapshot: std::fs::read("snapshot.json")?,
    targets: BTreeMap::from([
        ("targets".to_owned(), std::fs::read("targets.json")?),
        ("stable".to_owned(), std::fs::read("stable.json")?),
    ]),
};
// The length and SHA-256 of the file you downloaded.
let artifact = Artifact { length, hashes: BTreeMap::from([("sha256".to_owned(), sha256_hex)]) };

let verified = verify(&trusted, &fetched, "stable/app-1.0-aarch64-darwin.tar", &artifact, SystemTime::now())?;
// Install the artifact, and keep verified.trusted for the next update.
```

`verify` opens no file and no connection and reads no clock: you pass the
time in. When it refuses, the error names the role whose check failed, the
rule, and for a threshold every signatory with how they stood: who signed and
did not count, and why.

A target's path is an audience's name and a file name, such as
`stable/app-1.0-aarch64-darwin.tar`. The top-level targets role delegates
each audience to its own role and its own signers, so a release signed for
one audience never installs for another.

## Sign as a maintainer

The `x0k-release-metadata` program runs the signing ceremony. One maintainer
stages a new root or targets file. Each signer signs it on their own machine,
with their own key, in any order. The status names who is still missing.

```sh
cargo install x0k-release-metadata
x0k-release-metadata stage 2.root.body.json 2.root.json
x0k-release-metadata sign 2.root.json --trusted 1.root.json --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk
x0k-release-metadata status 2.root.json --trusted 1.root.json
```

A first root, version 1, is signed the same way, without `--trusted`.
`sign` takes several staged files and signs them with one signature, so a
security key is touched once, for example a new root and the targets file
under it:

```sh
x0k-release-metadata sign 2.root.json targets.json --trusted 1.root.json --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk
```

A maintainer whose key the root also lists for the snapshot and the
timestamp releases with one touch. `release` signs the audience's targets
file, writes the snapshot and the timestamp, and signs all three together:

```sh
x0k-release-metadata release stable.json --trusted root.json --delegator targets.json \
    --targets targets.json --snapshot snapshot.json --timestamp timestamp.json \
    --snapshot-expires-in 7d --timestamp-expires-in 1d --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk \
    --rebuilt stable/app-1.0-aarch64-darwin.tar=target/app-1.0-aarch64-darwin.tar
```

From Rust, `sign_release` does the same in one call. The build server
signs the snapshot and the timestamp with its one online key, and a
scheduled job refreshes the timestamp with one command:

```sh
x0k-release-metadata timestamp timestamp.json --trusted root.json --snapshot snapshot.json \
    --previous timestamp.json --expires-in 1d --key online_ed25519
```

The program holds no key. It signs through `ssh-keygen -Y sign`, or any
program with the same interface that you name with `--signer`. A new root
needs the signatures of the old root's signatories and of its own. A targets
file is signed only against your own rebuild of each artifact
(`--rebuilt <path>=<file>`), or with `--not-reproducible` where the build is
not reproducible.

## The schemes

| Scheme | Signer |
|---|---|
| `ed25519` | TUF's own: a software key |
| `sshsig-ssh-ed25519` | An SSH key |
| `sshsig-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` | A Secure Enclave key through Secretive |
| `sshsig-sk-ssh-ed25519` | A FIDO2 security key |
| `sshsig-sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` | A FIDO2 security key, or a passkey through WebAuthn |

Every scheme is verified in the process, by this crate. Nothing runs
`ssh-keygen` to verify. Every scheme can also make a batch signature: one
signature over a statement that lists several files by type, role,
version and hash, which counts on each file it lists.

## What it promises

This is release 0.3. What you may rely on is written down in
[the release-metadata decision](decisions/architecture/delivery/release-metadata.md):
the record formats, the rules a reader checks, and what each refusal means.
What it does not protect against, and what it assumes, is in
[THREAT-MODEL.md](THREAT-MODEL.md); read it before you sign your first root.

`crates/x0k-release-metadata/vectors/` holds the conformance vectors: small signed
repositories on disk, each with the verdict a reader must reach. Another
implementation can run the same files. `cargo test` runs them here. The
vectors whose names begin with `hw-` were signed once by real devices, a
FIDO2 key, a Secure Enclave key and a phone passkey; the others are signed by
software keys from fixed seeds, and `cargo run --example make_vectors --
vectors`, run in `crates/x0k-release-metadata/`, writes them again byte for
byte. The `tuf-` vectors use TUF's own scheme only, and
`crates/x0k-release-metadata/interop/run.sh` checks that python-tuf and go-tuf
reach the same verdict on each.

## Reading the implementation

The Rust here is written as chapters under `implementation/`, which explain
the code and generate it. Change the chapter, not the generated file.

**What it ships.** Every chapter, grouped by what it is about rather than which crate its code lands in.

### The verifier

The metadata types, the schemes, counting signatories, and the client workflow.

- [x0k-release-metadata: verifying a release against its maintainers](implementation/release-metadata/release-metadata.md) — The TUF metadata types with signatory, custody and presence-flag fields, TUF's ed25519 scheme and the four SSHSIG schemes (an SSH key, a Secure Enclave key, a FIDO2 token, a passkey through WebAuthn), batch signatures that count on every file their statement lists, and a pure verifier that walks TUF's client workflow and counts signatories, not keys.

### The conformance vectors

Each claim of the decision as a signed repository on disk, and the generator that writes them.

- [The conformance vectors of x0k-release-metadata](implementation/release-metadata/vectors.md) — Signed repositories on disk, one per claim of the release-metadata decision, each with the outcome the verifier must reach, and the generator that writes them.

### The signing ceremony

The stage, sign and status commands, the signer program, and the rebuild check.

- [The signing ceremony of x0k-release-metadata](implementation/release-metadata/ceremony.md) — The stage, sign and status commands of the release-metadata ceremony: a root or targets file is staged once, each signatory signs it on their own machine through a signer program with ssh-keygen's interface, several files at once with one batch signature, the status names who is missing, a targets entry is signed only when it matches the signer's own rebuild, and a release's targets file, snapshot and timestamp take one signature.

### The hardware signing kit

How the vectors signed by real devices are made.

- [The hardware signing kit of x0k-release-metadata](implementation/release-metadata/hardware-kit.md) — The kit an operator runs once on a Mac to make one conformance vector per hardware scheme, signed by the real signer: fresh FIDO2 keys through ssh-keygen, a fresh Secure Enclave key through Secretive, and a passkey through a local WebAuthn page, each signed through the crate's own ceremony, one file at a time or two files with one batch signature.

## Where it comes from

This repository is projected from [x0k](https://0k.computer), a local-first
system whose releases it verifies. A change proposed here comes back as a
proposal against x0k's sources and appears in this repository on the next
projection.
